claim: Compensatory intact hand usage after amputation facilitates remapping of limb representations in the cortical territory of the missing hand.
source: Previously we showed, using task-evoked fMRI, that compensatory intact hand usage after amputation facilitates remapping of limb representations in the cortical territory of the missing hand (Makin et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Makin et al., 2013a)

claim: Compensatory arm usage in individuals born without a hand reflects functional connectivity of spontaneous brain activity in the cortical hand region.
source: Here we show that compensatory arm usage in individuals born without a hand (one-handers) reflects functional connectivity of spontaneous brain activity in the cortical hand region.
evidence: This is a primary finding claim supported by the data presented in the manuscript

claim: One-handers showed reduced symmetry of hand region inter-hemispheric resting-state functional connectivity compared with two-handed controls.
source: Compared with two-handed controls, one-handers showed reduced symmetry of hand region inter-hemispheric resting-state functional connectivity and corticospinal white matter microstructure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: One-handers showed reduced symmetry of corticospinal white matter microstructure compared with two-handed controls.
source: Compared with two-handed controls, one-handers showed reduced symmetry of hand region inter-hemispheric resting-state functional connectivity and corticospinal white matter microstructure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: One-handers who more frequently use their residual arm for typically bimanual daily tasks showed more symmetrical functional connectivity of the hand region.
source: Nevertheless, those one-handers who more frequently use their residual (handless) arm for typically bimanual daily tasks also showed more symmetrical functional connectivity of the hand region, demonstrating that adaptive behaviour drives long-range brain organisation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation between behavior and connectivity

claim: Adaptive behaviour drives long-range brain organisation in one-handers.
source: Nevertheless, those one-handers who more frequently use their residual (handless) arm for typically bimanual daily tasks also showed more symmetrical functional connectivity of the hand region, demonstrating that adaptive behaviour drives long-range brain organisation.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between compensatory behavior and brain connectivity patterns

claim: Compensatory arm usage maintains symmetrical sensorimotor functional connectivity in one-handers.
source: We therefore suggest that compensatory arm usage maintains symmetrical sensorimotor functional connectivity in one-handers.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the observed correlation between arm usage and connectivity

claim: Variability in spontaneous functional connectivity reflects ecological behaviour.
source: Since variability in spontaneous functional connectivity in our study reflects ecological behaviour, we propose that inter-hemispheric symmetry, typically observed in resting sensorimotor networks, depends on coordinated motor behaviour in daily life.
evidence: Based on the observed relationship between daily arm usage and resting-state connectivity

claim: Inter-hemispheric symmetry typically observed in resting sensorimotor networks depends on coordinated motor behaviour in daily life.
source: Since variability in spontaneous functional connectivity in our study reflects ecological behaviour, we propose that inter-hemispheric symmetry, typically observed in resting sensorimotor networks, depends on coordinated motor behaviour in daily life.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the study findings

claim: The relationship between deprivation-triggered brain plasticity and adaptive behaviour following visual loss has been a focus of much research and debate.
source: The relationship between deprivation-triggered brain plasticity and adaptive behaviour following visual loss has been a focus of much research and debate (Merabet and Pascual-Leone, 2010; Baseler et al., 2011; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: A link between brain plasticity following amputation and compensatory behaviour has only recently been established.
source: In the sensorimotor system, a link between brain plasticity following amputation and compensatory behaviour has only recently been established (Makin et al., 2013a; Philip and Frey, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work

claim: Research on behavioural changes in people born without a hand has focused on compensatory foot usage.
source: In people who were born without a hand, or who lost it in childhood, research on related behavioural changes has focused on compensatory foot usage (which is uncommon relative to arm usage), with conflicting results (Yu et al., 2006; Stoeckel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Compensatory foot usage is uncommon relative to arm usage in people born without a hand.
source: In people who were born without a hand, or who lost it in childhood, research on related behavioural changes has focused on compensatory foot usage (which is uncommon relative to arm usage), with conflicting results (Yu et al., 2006; Stoeckel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The way individuals use their bodies to compensate for their disability when missing a hand is reflected in the way the cortical territory of the missing hand is recruited during limb movements.
source: We recently showed using task-evoked fMRI that the way individuals use their bodies to compensate for their disability when missing a hand (either at birth or later in life due to injury) is reflected in the way the cortical territory of the missing hand is recruited during limb movements (Makin et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Individuals born with one hand showed both higher usage of the handless arm in daily tasks and increased activation in the cortical territory of the missing hand when moving that arm.
source: Specifically, individuals born with one hand (i.e., congenital unilateral upper limb absence; hereafter termed: 'one handers') showed both higher usage of the handless arm (i.e., residual arm) in daily tasks and increased activation in the cortical territory of the missing hand when moving that arm.
evidence: This refers to findings from prior work by the authors

claim: Amputees that lost a hand later in life tended to use their remaining hand more frequently and showed greater activation in the territory of the missing hand when moving the intact hand.
source: In contrast, amputees that lost a hand later in life tended to use their remaining hand (i.e., intact hand) more frequently and also showed greater activation in the territory of the missing hand when moving the intact hand.
evidence: This refers to findings from prior work by the authors

claim: Whichever body part is being over-used to compensate for the absence of a hand gains increased representation in the cortical territory of the missing hand.
source: These results provide evidence that whichever body part is being over-used to compensate for the absence of a hand also gains increased representation in the cortical territory of the missing hand.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior findings cited in the text

claim: Changes in brain activity underlying task performance may be captured indirectly by measuring spontaneous fluctuations in fMRI signal while participants are resting in the scanner.
source: Changes in brain activity underlying task performance may also be captured indirectly by measuring spontaneous fluctuations in fMRI signal while participants are not performing a task, but are instead resting in the scanner (Gilaie-Dotan et al., 2013; Harmelech and Malach, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: During rest, the human brain is characterised by activation patterns that are temporally coherent and reproducible across known functional networks.
source: During rest, the human brain is characterised by activation patterns that are temporally coherent and reproducible across known functional networks, and this coherence is termed 'functional connectivity' (Biswal et al., 1995; Nir et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2009; Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: The relationship between altered resting-state functional connectivity and compensatory behaviour in one-handers was not known prior to this study.
source: To date, the relationship between altered resting-state functional connectivity and compensatory behaviour in one-handers is not known (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation indicating gap in knowledge

claim: Patterns of resting-state functional connectivity reflect the activity patterns evoked by every-day behaviours.
source: Since it has been hypothesised that patterns of resting-state functional connectivity reflect the activity patterns evoked by every-day behaviours (Harmelech and Malach, 2013), we predicted that the way individuals behave to compensate for their disability would also be reflected in resting-state connectivity patterns.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature cited in the text

claim: Inter-hemispheric functional connectivity patterns are stronger between homologous regions along the sensorimotor homunculus, resulting in a symmetrical connectivity pattern.
source: We focused on inter-hemispheric functional connectivity patterns, which are stronger between homologous regions along the sensorimotor homunculus, resulting in a symmetrical connectivity pattern.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about brain organization

claim: One-handers have a more asymmetrical pattern of limb use in daily life compared to controls.
source: We aimed to test whether this symmetry is disrupted in one-handers who have a more asymmetrical pattern of limb use in daily life (i.e., increased usage of their intact hand vs their residual arm).
evidence: This is an assumption based on the nature of the condition

claim: The study included 14 one-handers and 23 two-handed controls.
source: Here we identified atypical asymmetry in functional connectivity and in structural features (as measured by white matter microstructure) in a relatively large sample of one-handers (n = 14, see Table 1 for demographic details) compared with matched two-handed controls (n = 23).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample

claim: The degree of functional connectivity between the two homologous hand regions in the sensorimotor cortex reflected the degree to which one-handers utilised their residual arm during daily activities.
source: Importantly, the degree of functional connectivity between the two homologous hand regions in the sensorimotor cortex reflected the degree to which one-handers utilised their residual arm during daily activities.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the data analysis

claim: Resting-state connectivity alterations reflect adaptive behaviours beyond the scope that could be identified using task-evoked brain activity.
source: These findings extend our previous reports by demonstrating that resting-state connectivity alterations reflect adaptive behaviours beyond the scope that could be identified using task-evoked brain activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in relation to prior work

claim: Daily behaviours are imprinted in spontaneous brain activity.
source: These findings also demonstrate the imprinting of daily behaviours in spontaneous brain activity, as previously postulated (Harmelech and Malach, 2013).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by the current data and prior hypothesis

claim: The corticospinal tracts mediate a range of descending pathways from cortical motor areas to the spinal cord, as well as ascending tracts to somatosensory cortex.
source: The corticospinal tracts mediate a range of descending pathways from cortical motor areas to the spinal cord, as well as ascending tracts to somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge

claim: Fractional anisotropy is an index commonly derived from diffusion MRI that is used as a probe of tissue microstructure.
source: Fractional anisotropy (FA), an index commonly derived from diffusion MRI, was used as a probe of tissue microstructure.
evidence: This is established methodological knowledge

claim: Fractional anisotropy is thought to reflect myelination and fibre density, but is also influenced by other micro-features.
source: This measurement is thought to reflect myelination and fibre density, but is also influenced by other micro-features (e.g., membrane permeability, tissue geometry, see 'Discussion') (Zatorre et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2013; Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on diffusion MRI

claim: One-handers showed increased asymmetry in white matter microstructure in the corticospinal tract contralateral to the missing hand relative to the ipsilateral tract compared to controls (p = 0.003).
source: One-handers showed increased asymmetry in white matter microstructure (reflected by decreased white matter FA in the corticospinal tract contralateral to the missing hand relative to the ipsilateral tract) compared to controls (p = 0.003, randomisation test, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and presented in Figure 1A

claim: The white matter asymmetry effect peaked at the posterior limb of the internal capsule (peak z coordinate = 88, p = 0.02 corrected).
source: The effect peaked at the posterior limb of the internal capsule (peak z coordinate = 88, p = 0.02 corrected, Figure 1B), an area that contains sensory thalamic fibres, but was also distributed across extensive regions of the tract (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and presented in Figure 1B

claim: The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains sensory thalamic fibres.
source: The effect peaked at the posterior limb of the internal capsule (peak z coordinate = 88, p = 0.02 corrected, Figure 1B), an area that contains sensory thalamic fibres, but was also distributed across extensive regions of the tract (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as anatomical knowledge

claim: No significant group differences were found for control tracts that are not directly associated with the sensorimotor system.
source: No significant group differences were found for control tracts that are not directly associated with the sensorimotor system (Inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus: p = 0.28, Inferior longitudinal fasciculus: p = 0.27, randomisation tests).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of control regions

claim: Accumulating evidence links white matter microstructure with motor behaviour.
source: Since accumulating evidence links white matter microstructure with motor behaviour (Scholz et al., 2009; Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2013), we aimed to test if asymmetry of white matter microstructure would be related to compensatory arm usage, as previously assessed (Makin et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: No significant relationship was found between white matter microstructure asymmetry and compensatory arm usage (r = −0.27, p = 0.17).
source: However, no significant relationship was found (r = −0.27, p = 0.17, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: In the typical brain, the sensorimotor system is characterised by high levels of inter-hemispheric functional connectivity between homologous brain areas, resulting in symmetrical connectivity patterns.
source: In the typical brain, the sensorimotor system is characterised by high levels of inter-hemispheric functional connectivity between homologous brain areas, resulting in symmetrical connectivity patterns (Biswal et al., 1995; Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Reduced connectivity to the seed-region was identified in the medial aspect of the homologous (intact) hand region, in the anterior bank of the central sulcus, corresponding with M1.
source: Reduced connectivity to the seed-region was identified in the medial aspect of the homologous (intact) hand region, in the anterior bank of the central sulcus, corresponding with M1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and presented in Figure 2B

claim: The reduced connectivity finding reflects an aberration in the typically symmetrical resting-state sensorimotor network.
source: This finding reflects an aberration in the typically symmetrical resting-state sensorimotor network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity findings

claim: Group comparison confirmed reduced connectivity between the two sensorimotor hand regions (p = 0.002).
source: Group comparison of inter-hemispheric connectivity in the intact hand region, defined based on brain activations during hand movements, confirmed reduced connectivity between the two sensorimotor hand regions (p = 0.002, randomisation test, middle panel of Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and presented in Figure 2B

claim: Smaller clusters showing reductions in connectivity with the seed-region were identified in the posterior aspect of the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex contralateral to the missing hand and in the middle temporal gyrus bilaterally.
source: Smaller Clusters showing reductions in connectivity with the seed-region were also identified in the posterior aspect of the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex contralateral to the missing hand and in the middle temporal gyrus bilaterally (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and presented in Table 2

claim: No differences were found in the variance of the mean regional time-course between one-handers and controls (p = 0.5).
source: No differences were found in the variance of both the mean regional time-course (p = 0.5, randomisation test), or the mean single-voxel time-courses (p = 0.5, randomisation test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: No differences were found in the variance of the mean single-voxel time-courses between one-handers and controls (p = 0.5).
source: No differences were found in the variance of both the mean regional time-course (p = 0.5, randomisation test), or the mean single-voxel time-courses (p = 0.5, randomisation test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: The missing hand territory of one-handers is activated when one-handers move their residual arm.
source: We have previously shown that the missing hand territory of one-handers is activated when one-handers move their residual arm.
evidence: This refers to prior findings by the authors

claim: Significant correlation between functional connectivity values and residual arm usage was found in a single cluster within the intact cortical hand region, specifically in the anterior bank of the central sulcus, corresponding with M1.
source: Significant correlation with behavioural scores was found in a single cluster within the intact cortical hand region (Figure 2C), specifically in the anterior bank of the central sulcus, corresponding with M1.
evidence: Supported by data analysis and presented in Figure 2C

claim: One-handers who employ their residual arm for typically bimanual tasks demonstrate higher levels of hand region inter-hemispheric connectivity.
source: This result indicates that one-handers who employ their residual arm for typically bimanual tasks also demonstrate higher levels of hand region inter-hemispheric connectivity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis

claim: The more one-handers utilised their residual arm in daily tasks, the higher the inter-hemispheric connectivity between their cortical hand regions (r = 0.66, p = 0.004).
source: A correlation analysis confirmed that the more one-handers utilised their residual arm in daily tasks, the higher the inter-hemispheric connectivity between their cortical hand regions (r = 0.66, p = 0.004, randomisation test, middle panel of Figure 2C), resulting in relatively normal (symmetrical) patterns of inter-hemispheric connectivity in the individuals that adaptively use their residual arm.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and presented in Figure 2C

claim: Individuals that adaptively use their residual arm show relatively normal (symmetrical) patterns of inter-hemispheric connectivity.
source: A correlation analysis confirmed that the more one-handers utilised their residual arm in daily tasks, the higher the inter-hemispheric connectivity between their cortical hand regions (r = 0.66, p = 0.004, randomisation test, middle panel of Figure 2C), resulting in relatively normal (symmetrical) patterns of inter-hemispheric connectivity in the individuals that adaptively use their residual arm.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings

claim: The cross-sectional nature of this study prevents determination of the origin of the increased functional connectivity observed in those who used their residual arm more frequently.
source: Due to the cross-sectional nature of this study, we are unable to determine the origin of the increased functional connectivity observed in those who used their residual arm more frequently.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study design

claim: The increased functional connectivity may reflect preservation of initially intact inter-regional connections, which are otherwise lost through lack of use.
source: This observation may reflect preservation of initially intact inter-regional connections, which are otherwise lost through lack of use, or may instead reflect establishment of (otherwise missing) functional connections through usage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings

claim: The increased functional connectivity may reflect establishment of (otherwise missing) functional connections through usage.
source: This observation may reflect preservation of initially intact inter-regional connections, which are otherwise lost through lack of use, or may instead reflect establishment of (otherwise missing) functional connections through usage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings

claim: The fact that individuals with increased functional connectivity didn't also show greater structural symmetry may support the interpretation of functional reorganisation.
source: The fact that individuals with increased functional connectivity didn't also show greater structural symmetry may support the latter interpretation of functional reorganisation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissociation between structural and functional findings

claim: Compensatory behaviour is a powerful driver in shaping brain organisation associated with sensorimotor deprivation, as reflected in resting-state functional connectivity.
source: Either way, our findings suggest that compensatory behaviour is a powerful driver in shaping brain organisation associated with sensorimotor deprivation, as reflected in resting-state functional connectivity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings

claim: Individualised ecological behaviour is imprinted in spontaneous brain connectivity patterns.
source: Our unique dataset also provides a rare opportunity to demonstrate how individualised ecological behaviour is imprinted in spontaneous brain connectivity patterns, as was previously hypothesised (Harmelech and Malach, 2013).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by the current data and prior hypothesis

claim: White matter in one-handers was relatively reduced along the corticospinal tract contralateral to the missing hand, compared to the homologous tract contralateral to the intact hand.
source: White matter in one-handers was relatively reduced along the corticospinal tract contralateral to the missing hand, compared to the homologous tract contralateral to the intact hand.
evidence: This is a summary of the white matter findings

claim: The white matter measurement FA is an indirect and relatively unspecific measure of white matter microstructure.
source: The white matter measurement used here (FA) is an indirect and relatively unspecific measure of white matter microstructure (Zatorre et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to methodological literature

claim: FA reflects how directional water diffusion is within tissue, due to presence of structural barriers.
source: It reflects how directional water diffusion is within tissue, due to presence of structural barriers.
evidence: This is an explanation of the FA measurement

claim: The more coherent structural barriers are, the higher the degree of diffusion directionality (FA) will be.
source: The more coherent these barriers are, the higher the degree of diffusion directionality, that is, FA, will be.
evidence: This is an explanation of the FA measurement

claim: Many different features, including the degree of myelination, the fibre packing density, the membrane permeability, axon diameter and the tissue geometry, could influence the reported structural asymmetry.
source: Many different features, including the degree of myelination, the fibre packing density, the membrane permeability, axon diameter and the tissue geometry, could therefore influence the reported structural asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated as methodological knowledge about FA interpretation

claim: The maturation and refinement of corticospinal pathways crucially depends on motor behaviour and the neural activity it elicits in early life.
source: Our observation is in line with numerous studies showing that the maturation and refinement of corticospinal pathways crucially depends on motor behaviour and the neural activity it elicits in early life (Eyre, 2007; Martin et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Asymmetry of white matter microstructure in the posterior limb of the internal capsule has been previously shown to predict poor motor function of the upper limb after stroke.
source: Similarly, asymmetry of white matter microstructure in the posterior limb of the internal capsule has been previously shown to predict poor motor function of the upper limb after stroke (Stinear et al., 2007; Lotze et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Reduced motor behaviour and subsequent neuronal activity in one-handers may result in decreased white matter microstructure in the corticospinal tract contralateral to the missing hand.
source: According to this account, reduced motor behaviour and subsequent neuronal activity in one-handers may result in decreased white matter microstructure in the corticospinal tract contralateral to the missing hand.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior literature

claim: A reduction in hand-region inter-hemispheric functional connectivity was previously reported in acquired amputees, associated with phantom pain.
source: We previously reported a reduction in hand-region inter-hemispheric functional connectivity in acquired amputees, that was associated with phantom pain (Makin et al., 2013b): individuals suffering from worse chronic phantom pain showed greater asymmetry in inter-hemispheric functional connectivity.
evidence: This refers to prior findings by the authors

claim: Individuals suffering from worse chronic phantom pain showed greater asymmetry in inter-hemispheric functional connectivity.
source: We previously reported a reduction in hand-region inter-hemispheric functional connectivity in acquired amputees, that was associated with phantom pain (Makin et al., 2013b): individuals suffering from worse chronic phantom pain showed greater asymmetry in inter-hemispheric functional connectivity.
evidence: This refers to prior findings by the authors

claim: Reductions in functional connectivity in acquired amputees may relate to abnormal signalling of the peripheral injured nerve.
source: We proposed that reductions in functional connectivity may relate to abnormal signalling of the peripheral injured nerve (Vaso et al., 2014), which could reduce the synchronicity of fluctuations between the bilateral hand regions.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation supported by citation

claim: Abnormal signalling of the peripheral injured nerve could reduce the synchronicity of fluctuations between the bilateral hand regions.
source: We proposed that reductions in functional connectivity may relate to abnormal signalling of the peripheral injured nerve (Vaso et al., 2014), which could reduce the synchronicity of fluctuations between the bilateral hand regions.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on inference

claim: One-handers rarely experience phantom sensations.
source: In the one-handers studied here, who rarely experience phantom sensations (Price, 2006), the observed reduction in inter-hemispheric connectivity may instead be related to the strong and chronic lateralisation of motor behaviour, resulting in dis-synchronisation of inputs between the two hand regions, as will be discussed below.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The observed reduction in inter-hemispheric connectivity in one-handers may be related to the strong and chronic lateralisation of motor behaviour, resulting in dis-synchronisation of inputs between the two hand regions.
source: In the one-handers studied here, who rarely experience phantom sensations (Price, 2006), the observed reduction in inter-hemispheric connectivity may instead be related to the strong and chronic lateralisation of motor behaviour, resulting in dis-synchronisation of inputs between the two hand regions, as will be discussed below.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings

claim: High residual-arm users jointly activate the missing hand territory (through residual arm movements) and the intact hand cortex (through intact hand movements) in everyday settings.
source: Based on our previous and current findings, we suggest that 'high' residual-arm users jointly activate the missing hand territory (through residual arm movements, consequential to adaptive plasticity) and the intact hand cortex (through intact hand movements) in everyday settings, such as while performing typically bimanual tasks.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the current and prior findings

claim: Repeated cortical activations are imprinted into resting-state connectivity patterns.
source: These repeated cortical activations are imprinted into resting-state connectivity patterns (Harmelech and Malach, 2013; Guerra-Carrillo et al., 2014), and are therefore reflected as symmetrical levels of inter-hemispheric connectivity in these individuals.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The current study highlights the pivotal role of the missing hand's cortical territory in use-dependent plasticity.
source: The current study therefore highlights the pivotal role of the missing hand's cortical territory in use-dependent plasticity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the overall findings

claim: Significant group differences in functional connectivity were not entirely exclusive to the intact hand region.
source: We note that significant group differences in functional connectivity were not entirely exclusive to the intact hand region (e.g., prefrontal cortex, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 2

claim: Effects in cortical areas beyond the intact hand region were not related to compensatory behaviour.
source: However, effects in these other cortical areas were not related to compensatory behaviour (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data analysis presented in Figure 2C

claim: Lateralised activation patterns are evoked by unimanual movements.
source: In contrast to lateralised activation patterns evoked by unimanual movements, resting-state patterns typically show strong bilateral coherence, resulting in highly symmetrical networks (Biswal et al., 1995; Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Resting-state patterns typically show strong bilateral coherence, resulting in highly symmetrical networks.
source: In contrast to lateralised activation patterns evoked by unimanual movements, resting-state patterns typically show strong bilateral coherence, resulting in highly symmetrical networks (Biswal et al., 1995; Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Reduced bimanual movements (in the absence of one hand, and with limited compensatory capacity of the residual arm) is related to decreased inter-hemispheric coherence in one-handers.
source: Our observation that reduced bimanual movements (in the absence of one hand, and with limited compensatory capacity of the residual arm) is related to decreased inter-hemispheric coherence in one-handers, provides compelling new evidence that the symmetrical resting-state coherence typically found in the sensorimotor network is likely to be due to coordinated body movements in naturalistic daily settings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study findings

claim: The symmetrical resting-state coherence typically found in the sensorimotor network is likely to be due to coordinated body movements in naturalistic daily settings.
source: Our observation that reduced bimanual movements (in the absence of one hand, and with limited compensatory capacity of the residual arm) is related to decreased inter-hemispheric coherence in one-handers, provides compelling new evidence that the symmetrical resting-state coherence typically found in the sensorimotor network is likely to be due to coordinated body movements in naturalistic daily settings.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the study findings

claim: Spontaneous coherence seen in brain networks during rest relates to the relatively integrated activity of network sub-regions during complex real-life behaviours.
source: We therefore propose that spontaneous coherence seen in brain networks during rest (Nir et al., 2006) relates to the relatively integrated activity of network sub-regions during complex real-life behaviours.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the findings

claim: Data from one control participant were discarded from the resting states fMRI analyses due to excessive head movements (>3 mm).
source: Data from one control participant were discarded from the resting states fMRI analysese due to excessive head movements (>3 mm), and data from a different control participant were discarded from diffusion MRI analyses due to problems during data collection.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data exclusion

claim: Data from a different control participant were discarded from diffusion MRI analyses due to problems during data collection.
source: Data from one control participant were discarded from the resting states fMRI analysese due to excessive head movements (>3 mm), and data from a different control participant were discarded from diffusion MRI analyses due to problems during data collection.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data exclusion

claim: Three one-handers and three control participants were additionally recruited beyond the previous study sample.
source: Additionally, three one-handers and three control participants were recruited, resulting in a total of 14 one-handers (age = 36.64 ± 12.02, four with absent right hand, see Table 1 for demographic details) and 24 controls (age = 41.12 ± 12.86, eight left hand dominant).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant recruitment

claim: The final sample included 14 one-handers (age = 36.64 ± 12.02, four with absent right hand) and 24 controls (age = 41.12 ± 12.86, eight left hand dominant).
source: Additionally, three one-handers and three control participants were recruited, resulting in a total of 14 one-handers (age = 36.64 ± 12.02, four with absent right hand, see Table 1 for demographic details) and 24 controls (age = 41.12 ± 12.86, eight left hand dominant).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the final sample, with demographic details in Table 1

claim: Recruitment was carried through the Oxford Centre for Enablement and Opcare in accordance with NHS national research ethics service approval (10/H0707/29).
source: Recruitment was carried through the Oxford Centre for Enablement and Opcare in accordance with NHS national research ethics service approval (10/H0707/29), and written informed consent was obtained.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about ethics and recruitment

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
source: Recruitment was carried through the Oxford Centre for Enablement and Opcare in accordance with NHS national research ethics service approval (10/H0707/29), and written informed consent was obtained.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about ethics

claim: Use of residual arm and prosthesis in one-handers were assessed with a revised version of the Motor Activity Log.
source: Use of residual arm and prosthesis in one-handers were assessed with a revised version of the Motor Activity Log (Uswatte et al., 2006), as described before (Makin et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citations

claim: Participants with limb absence were requested to rate how frequently they incorporate their residual arm in an inventory of daily activities, with varying degrees of motor control.
source: In short, participants with limb absence were requested to rate how frequently they incorporate their residual arm (either directly, or using a prosthesis) in an inventory of daily activities, with varying degrees of motor control.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about behavioral assessment

claim: The bimanual usage questionnaire was previously validated using limb acceleration data, collected in ecological settings.
source: This questionnaire, indexing bimanual usage, was previously validated using limb acceleration data, collected in ecological settings (Makin et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior validation work

claim: The scanning protocol consisted of an anatomical T1 scan, a resting-state scan, a task-evoked scan for body-part functional localisation and two diffusion-weighted imaging scans.
source: The scanning protocol consisted of an anatomical T1 scan, a resting-state scan, a task-evoked scan for body-part functional localisation and two diffusion-weighted imaging scans.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the scanning protocol

claim: Resting state functional data were acquired using a three Tesla Verio scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany).
source: Resting state functional data, based on the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal, were acquired using a three Tesla Verio scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany), and using a multiple gradient echo-planar T2*-weighted pulse sequence, with the parameters: TR = 2410 ms; TE = 30 ms; flip angle = 90°; imaging matrix = 64 × 64; FOV = 192 mm axial slices.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data acquisition

claim: A total of 128 volumes were collected during the resting-state scan.
source: A total of 128 volumes were collected (Makin et al., 2013b).

claim: During the resting-state scan, participants were asked to lie still for 5 min in a dimmed room with their eyes open, and let their mind wander.
